title: Briseno v. ConAgra Foods, Inc.
lead: Consumers challenge Wesson oil’s natural label, but many buyers lack receipts for the small purchases. The certification appeal asks whether a workable identification method is an extra threshold beyond Rule 23’s stated requirements.

actors.name: Wesson-oil consumers
actors.role: Plaintiffs seeking eleven statewide purchaser classes.

actors.name: ConAgra Foods, Inc.
actors.role: Manufacturer and seller challenging certification based on membership identification.

proceedings: The district court partly granted certification of eleven damages classes under Rule 23(b)(3).
The Ninth Circuit took interlocutory review under Rule 23(f) and affirmed rejection of a separate administrative-feasibility requirement.
limits: This account transforms the complete published opinion’s canonical brief without a fresh audit or current circuit-law survey. The concurrent memorandum addressing other certification objections is outside this account. Neither label illegality nor a particular distribution plan or every aspect of aggregate damages was finally decided here.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Buyers challenge the label on inexpensive grocery purchases
sections.cue: Why was identifying the class disputed?
paragraphs: ConAgra manufactured and sold Wesson cooking oils labeled “100% Natural.” Consumers alleged that the label was false or misleading because the oils contained genetically modified ingredients. Consolidated suits asserted state-law claims in eleven states and sought classes of residents who bought the products during the relevant periods.

The district court partly granted certification, creating eleven damages classes under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(3). ConAgra objected that grocery shoppers usually did not retain receipts and might not remember particular inexpensive purchases. The court required an objective purchase-based definition but refused to require a separate administratively feasible identification method. ConAgra obtained interlocutory review under Rule 23(f).

sections.title: The panel begins with the rule’s actual requirements
sections.cue: Why avoid a freestanding identification hurdle?
paragraphs: Judge Friedland wrote for a Ninth Circuit panel with Judges William A. Fletcher and Morgan B. Christen. It confined the published decision to whether administrative feasibility was an independent certification prerequisite. The court avoided “ascertainability,” a term used elsewhere for differing questions such as objective boundaries, vagueness, and definitions dependent on success on the merits.

Rule 23(a) expressly listed numerosity, commonality, typicality, and adequacy, without administrative feasibility. Rule 23(b)(3), by contrast, supplied an inclusive list of matters relevant to predominance and superiority and already directed consideration of management difficulties. Adding an independent threshold would enlarge the prescribed prerequisites while displacing their balancing process.

The Supreme Court’s Amchem decision cautioned against replacing the rulemaking process with judicially invented certification standards. Existing Rule 23 requirements remained mandatory and could address defective definitions; rejecting the extra hurdle did not relieve plaintiffs of proving them.

sections.title: Management and notice concerns remain part of existing safeguards
sections.cue: Why did the court reject categorical treatment of those burdens?
paragraphs: Management difficulties belonged in superiority’s comparison with other available methods, aided where appropriate by subclasses or issue certification. An isolated threshold could defeat low-value consumer claims even where separate suits offered no realistic alternative. The rule called for comparing costs and benefits.

For absent members, Rule 23 required the best practicable notice, including individual notice to those reasonably identifiable, rather than actual notice to everyone. Due process also permitted suitable alternative methods. In small-value cases, unidentified members had little economically realistic individual-litigation opportunity to lose. Perfect-identification demands could preserve a theoretical opportunity while preventing recovery altogether. The court’s discussion of cy pres distribution of residual funds supported that reasoning; it approved no specific distribution plan here.

Possible false claims and dilution could be managed through audits, administrators, sampling, follow-up communications, and tailored procedures. Low participation might further reduce dilution. Effects on residual cy pres funds after legitimate claimants were paid were distinct. Fraud and deficient notice could still matter; the court rejected making them the basis of an automatic additional prerequisite.

sections.title: ConAgra retains opportunities to challenge both liability and payment claims
sections.cue: How might aggregate damages differ from distribution?
paragraphs: ConAgra could dispute standing, representatives’ purchases and credibility, certification elements, substantive liability, and individual claims for payment. Certification did not change substantive burdens or require believing every assertion. Audits and, when appropriate, limited discovery from absent members could preserve defenses. Due process required a fair chance to contest claims, not the least expensive identification method at certification.

The consumers proposed measuring an aggregate price premium attributable to the label and multiplying it by units sold. If legally supportable, that method could separate total liability from deciding who received distributions. The panel used the proposal to show why recipient identification did not necessarily fix aggregate liability; it did not finally validate every aspect of the model. A clear class definition could also support later preclusion even without identifying all members at certification.

sections.title: The refusal to impose the extra test is affirmed
sections.cue: What remained outside this published ruling?
paragraphs: On January 3, 2017, the panel affirmed the district court’s refusal to condition certification on an independent administrative-feasibility showing. No judge wrote separately. The opinion described agreement with the Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits and differences from the Third Circuit and qualifications elsewhere, reflecting the landscape it addressed in 2017.

Other certification challenges were resolved in a concurrently filed memorandum, not in this published opinion. The panel did not decide that genetically modified ingredients were unnatural or that ConAgra’s label was unlawful. Those remained merits questions.
